Test a Specified Markov Transition Probability

Source: R/05_ht.R
test_prob.Rd

Test the null hypothesis that a single transition probability equals p0, against a two-sided alternative, using the asymptotic test of Anderson and Goodman (1957).

Usage

test_prob(x, ij, p0)

Arguments

x

An atomic vector or factor of states in time order, or an atomic matrix with one independent trajectory per row and common observation times in columns. Each path must have at least two observations; matrices must have at least one row. Missing values are not allowed. Validated by the internal validate_trajectories() helper.

ij

An atomic vector or factor of length two, with no dimensions or missing values. Its first entry is the source state and its second is the destination state. Both must occur in x. Entries are state values, not positions in the state space; equal entries test a self-transition.

p0

A single finite numeric probability strictly between zero and one. Boundary nulls are excluded because the asymptotic null variance vanishes there.

Value

An object of class htest, printed using the standard R test format, with components statistic (named X-squared), parameter (one degree of freedom), p.value, estimate, null.value, alternative ("two.sided"), method, and data.name. Additional components observed and expected contain the two-category observed and null expected transition counts.

Details

Section 3.1 (pp. 96–97) of Anderson and Goodman (1957) derives tests for specified transition probabilities from their multinomial asymptotic law. For a single entry, aggregate destinations into state \(j\) and its complement. Writing \(N_i\) for the number of departures from state \(i\), \(N_{ij}\) for transitions from \(i\) to \(j\), and \(\widehat p_{ij}=N_{ij}/N_i\), the two-category version of Equation (3.1) is $$X^2 = \frac{N_i(\widehat p_{ij}-p_0)^2}{p_0(1-p_0)}.$$ Under the null, this has an asymptotic chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom. No continuity correction is applied. The final observation is not counted as a departure; an error is raised if the source state has no observed departures.

The model is a time-homogeneous, first-order finite Markov chain. For a single long trajectory, the approximation requires adequate visits to the source state, as under the ergodic setting discussed in Section 5. It is not an exact binomial test conditional on the random departure count. For a matrix, rows are independent paths with a common transition matrix; counts are pooled across paths, excluding each path's final observation from departures. The Section 3.1 approximation applies as the number of independent paths increases with their common length fixed. A warning is issued if either null expected count, \(N_i p_0\) or \(N_i(1-p_0)\), is below five. The result reports a p-value rather than imposing a significance level; reject at level \(\alpha\) when the p-value is below \(\alpha\).

References

Anderson, T. W., and Goodman, L. A. (1957). Statistical Inference about Markov Chains. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 28(1), 89–110. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177707039 . See Section 3.1 for specified-probability tests and Section 5 for a single long chain.

See also

fit(), stats::chisq.test(), stats::prop.test()

Examples

x <- rep(c("a", "a", "b", "a", "b", "b"), 20)
test_prob(x, ij = c("a", "b"), p0 = 0.5)
#> 
#> 	Anderson-Goodman test of a transition probability
#> 
#> data:  x
#> X-squared = 6.6667, df = 1, p-value = 0.009823
#> alternative hypothesis: true p[a, b] is not equal to 0.5
#> sample estimates:
#>   p[a, b] 
#> 0.6666667 
#>
